context: Flat tetrahedra being falsely recognized as non-flat, which would then be incorrectly dealt with when subdividing Epstein–Penner triangulations into canonical triangulations. When the above issues arise in step 1, SnapPea/SnapPy fails to find the correct canonical triangulation and arrives at an incorrect one, while still representing the same manifold as the input triangulation. Hence steps 2 and 3 were necessary to spot and resolve these miscomputed cases. However, steps 2 and 3 can be very expensive to perform, and require back-and-forth adjustments of parameters. Furthermore, although successful for censuses with at most 9 tetrahedra, it is unknown whether step 3 will separate all cases within a computable scope, or even if it will separate all of them in theory [23]. ▶ Remark 10. We remark here that the subdividing algorithm Weeks implemented in SnapPea/SnapPy does not work for refinements of Epstein–Penner cellulations containing flat tetrahedra. This led to the miscomputed example x101 found by Burton [6] and mentioned in [22, Remark 3.6]. The cause of the miscomputation was not located at the time of [22]. During the course of this project, the author found another such example, o9_43806 and located the said cause. This bug has been fixed in SnapPy 3.3 by forcing it to find a refinement that does not contain flat tetrahedra before proceeding to subdividing it. After the fix, the numerical computation gives correct results for all minimal triangulations in the orientable cusped censuses of at most 10 tetrahedra, which we confirmed using the verified computation explained in Section 3.3.3 (as long as successfully computed). 3.3.3 Our method: verified computation Instead of making up for the mistakes caused by numerical computation of canonical triangulations using other methods, we enhance the computation itself to avoid the mistakes directly. With the accuracy issues described in the previous section, this requires us to: (a) given two supposedly different quantities, rigorously tell which one is larger; (b) given two supposedly equal quantities, prove that they are equal.

context: Throughout this paper, we assume triangulations consist of finitely many tetrahedra. If a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold admits an ideal triangulation, each tetrahedron has finite volume [15, §2.5], hence the volume of the manifold is finite. Conversely, any cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold has an ideal triangulation given by a refinement of the Epstein–Penner cellulation [37, §5]. Therefore, for cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, being finitevolume is equivalent to admitting ideal triangulations, hence we drop the term finite-volume when talking about cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds admitting ideal triangulations. In general, it is unknown whether all cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds admit geometric triangulations in the sense of Section 2.1 below [36]. However, when certifying hyperbolicity, SnapPy returns true if and only if it finds a geometric triangulation. Therefore an immediate corollary of this paper is that ▶ Corollary 2. All cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds ideally triangulable by at most 10 tetrahedra admit geometric triangulations. Note that nonorientable manifolds are included here since they are included in Theorem 7. For orientable manifolds, the above result can be strengthened to Proposition 11. We briefly review the needed terminologies in Section 2, then give detailed discussions in Section 3 for the creation of the 10-tetrahedra census, after which we give some applications of the extended census in Section 4. All corresponding code and data are available at [34]. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Triangulations A (generalised) triangulation T is a disjoint union of finitely many tetrahedra, with some or all faces identified in pairs via simplicial maps, and we avoid identifications where an edge is identified with itself in reverse. Note that T is not necessarily a simplicial complex, as identifications of two faces of the same tetrahedron are allowed.
